title: Find the largest / smallest element in an array (single pass, O(n)).
shortTitle: Find the Largest and Smallest Element in an Array

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the largest and smallest elements of an array is a single-pass linear scan. You initialise two tracking variables to the first element, then walk the rest of the array once, updating the maximum whenever you see a larger value and the minimum whenever you see a smaller value. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, and it is strictly better than sorting first, which would be N log N.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India has a list of the day's transaction amounts for Rajesh's account, and the fraud desk wants both the biggest and the smallest transaction. Instead of sorting the whole day's list, a clerk simply walks down the list once, remembering the biggest seen so far and the smallest seen so far, updating both as new amounts appear. By the end of one pass, the clerk has both answers.
s1_definition.oneliner: Seed max and min with the first element, then scan once, updating each when you see something bigger or smaller.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the largest and smallest elements of an array is a single-pass linear scan. You initialise two tracking variables to the first element, then walk the rest of the array once, updating the maximum whenever you see a larger value and the minimum whenever you see a smaller value. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, and it is strictly better than sorting first, which would be N log N.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India has a list of the day's transaction amounts for Rajesh's account, and the fraud desk wants both the biggest and the smallest transaction. Instead of sorting the whole day's list, a clerk simply walks down the list once, remembering the biggest seen so far and the smallest seen so far, updating both as new amounts appear. By the end of one pass, the clerk has both answers.

**One line to remember:** Seed max and min with the first element, then scan once, updating each when you see something bigger or smaller.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm starts by guarding the empty case, because an empty array has no largest or smallest, so you either throw an exception or return an empty result. For a non-empty array you initialise both max and min to the first element, not to zero and not to the extreme constant values, because seeding with the first real element is correct even when every element is negative, which matters for amounts that can represent debits.

Then you loop from the second element to the end. For each element you compare it against max and, if it is larger, update max; you compare it against min and, if it is smaller, update min. After the loop both variables hold the correct answers. This is a single pass, so it is linear in the number of elements.

A senior point is comparisons. The naive version does two comparisons per element. There is a classic optimisation that processes elements in pairs: compare the two elements of a pair first, then compare the larger against max and the smaller against min, which does three comparisons per two elements instead of four, reducing the comparison count by about a quarter. In an interview I mention this but note that the simple version is usually clearer and the difference rarely matters in practice.

Another senior point is the data type. For money I never use double because of rounding; I hold amounts in BigDecimal, and BigDecimal uses compareTo rather than the less-than operator, because equals on BigDecimal also considers scale while compareTo compares numeric value. So the comparison is written with compareTo returning a negative or positive number.

A third point is parallelism and streams. For very large arrays you can find the min and max with a parallel stream using summary statistics, but that has overhead and is only worth it for huge data; for typical sizes the simple sequential pass wins. I also prefer returning both results together in a small immutable result object rather than scanning twice, because scanning once is half the work.

A small finance-domain example: `BigDecimal max = amounts[0], min = amounts[0]; for (int i = 1; i < amounts.length; i++) { if (amounts[i].compareTo(max) > 0) max = amounts[i]; if (amounts[i].compareTo(min) < 0) min = amounts[i]; }` finds both the largest and smallest transaction in one pass.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India fraud desk reviews the day's transactions on Rajesh's account and needs the largest transaction, because an unusually large amount is a red flag, and the smallest transaction, because a tiny test transaction often precedes fraud. Finding both in one pass over the day's amounts is exactly this single-pass min-max scan.

This is exactly how the largest-and-smallest scan works in Java — we seed both trackers with the first amount and update them as we walk the list once.

Problem 2 — Amounts include debits represented as negative values and must be exact, so the code must use BigDecimal with compareTo rather than double, and it must handle an empty day gracefully by signalling that there is nothing to report rather than crashing. This shows the right data type and the empty-array guard.

What the code will do: an `ExtremesService` class with a `findExtremes(BigDecimal[] amounts)` method returning a small result holding both the maximum and minimum in a single pass, guarding the empty case. The demo scans a day of Rajesh's transactions and logs the biggest and smallest.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the day's amounts are `5000`, `-1200`, `89000`, `50`, and `-30000`.

Step 1: We guard the empty case; the array has five elements, so we proceed. We seed both max and min to the first element, `5000`. Seeding with a real element is why negatives are handled correctly.

Step 2: We look at `-1200`. It is not larger than `5000`, so max stays. It is smaller than `5000`, so min becomes `-1200`.

Step 3: We look at `89000`. It is larger than `5000`, so max becomes `89000`. It is not smaller than `-1200`, so min stays.

Step 4: We look at `50`. It is not larger than `89000`, so max stays. It is not smaller than `-1200`, so min stays.

Step 5: We look at `-30000`. It is not larger than `89000`, so max stays. It is smaller than `-1200`, so min becomes `-30000`.

Step 6: The loop ends. max is `89000` and min is `-30000`. We wrap them in an immutable Extremes result and return. The fraud desk sees the biggest credit and the biggest debit of the day from a single pass over the amounts.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T15:40:00Z INFO Largest=Rs.89000 Smallest=Rs.-30000
2026-10-26T15:40:00Z INFO Fraud review: biggest Rs.89000, smallest Rs.-30000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [5000, -1200, 89000, 50, -30000]
    │
    ▼
  seed max=5000, min=5000
    │ see -1200 → min=-1200
    │ see 89000 → max=89000
    │ see 50    → no change
    │ see -30000→ min=-30000
    ▼
  Extremes{max=89000, min=-30000}
    │
    ▼
  Output: fraud desk gets biggest credit & biggest debit (one pass)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the largest and smallest elements of an array is a single linear pass. I seed both a maximum and a minimum tracker with the first element, then I walk the rest of the array once, updating the maximum when I see a larger value and the minimum when I see a smaller value. One pass gives both answers in linear time with constant extra space, which beats sorting first because sorting is N log N.

A detail that matters is seeding. I seed with the first real element rather than zero or an extreme constant, because amounts can be negative when they represent debits, and seeding with zero would wrongly report zero as the minimum. I also guard the empty array, because there is no largest or smallest to report, and I signal that rather than crash.

For money I use BigDecimal and compare with compareTo, not the less-than operator, because BigDecimal equals also considers scale while compareTo compares numeric value. I mention the classic pairwise optimisation that cuts the comparison count by about a quarter by comparing elements in pairs before comparing against the trackers, though I note the simple version is usually clearer and I return both results together so I only scan once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the fraud desk, where the biggest transaction of the day is a red flag for an unusually large transfer and the smallest can be a tiny test transaction that often precedes fraud. Scanning the day's amounts once gives both, exactly, in BigDecimal, with negative debits handled correctly. Explaining the seeding choice, the data type, and the single-pass efficiency shows the interviewer that I write correct, efficient scans rather than reaching for a sort.
